<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_subsection"><a href="#S6.SS5" title="In VI Discussion and Ablation Study ‣ TFL: Targeted Bit-Flip Attack on Large Language Model" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_ref"><span class="ltx_text">VI-E</span> </span><span class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Runtime Analysis</span></span></a></li>
</ol></li>
<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_section"><a href="#S7" title="In TFL: Targeted Bit-Flip Attack on Large Language Model" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_ref">VII </span><span class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Potential Defense Discussion</span></span></a></li>
<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_section"><a href="#S8" title="In TFL: Targeted Bit-Flip Attack on Large Language Model" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_ref">VIII </span><span class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Conclusion</span></span></a></li>
<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_bibliography"><a href="#bib" title="In TFL: Targeted Bit-Flip Attack on Large Language Model" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title">References</span></a></li>
</ol></nav>

<article class="ltx_document ltx_authors_1line">
<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_font_bold ltx_title_document" style="font-size:144%;">TFL: <span id="id1" class="ltx_text ltx_underline">T</span>argeted Bit-<span id="id2" class="ltx_text ltx_underline">F</span>lip Attack on Large <span id="id3" class="ltx_text ltx_underline">L</span>anguage Model
</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Jingkai Guo  Chaitali Chakrabarti  Deliang Fan
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span><span id="id4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">School of Electrical, Computer and Energy Engineering</span>
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="id5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Arizona State University</span>
<br class="ltx_break">Tempe, AZ, USA 
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="id6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">{jingkaig,chaitali,dfan}@asu.edu</span>
</span></span></span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in safety and security critical applications, raising concerns about their robustness to model parameter fault injection attacks. Recent studies have shown that bit-flip attacks (BFAs), which exploit computer main memory (i.e., DRAM) vulnerabilities to flip a small number of bits in model weights, can severely disrupt LLM behavior <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>, <a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">2</a>, <a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>]</cite>. However, existing BFA on LLM largely induce un-targeted failure or general performance degradation, offering limited control over manipulating specific or targeted outputs. In this paper,
we present TFL, a novel targeted bit-flip attack framework that enables precise manipulation of LLM outputs for selected prompts while maintaining almost no or minor degradation on unrelated inputs. Within our TFL framework, we propose a novel keyword-focused attack loss to promote attacker-specified target tokens in generative outputs, together with an auxiliary utility score that balances attack effectiveness against collateral performance impact on benign data.
We evaluate TFL on multiple LLMs (Qwen, DeepSeek, Llama) and benchmarks (DROP, GSM8K, and TriviaQA). The experiments show that TFL achieves successful targeted LLM output manipulations with less than 50 bit flips and significantly reduced effect on unrelated queries compared to prior BFA approaches. This demonstrates the effectiveness of TFL and positions it as a new class of stealthy and targeted LLM model attack.</p>
  
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">I </span><span id="S1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Introduction</span></h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit strong performance across a broad range of tasks, including text comprehension, generation, translation, and reasoning. These capabilities stem primarily from large-scale pretraining on massive corpora, the adoption of transformer-based architectures, and favorable scaling laws, which together allow LLMs to learn rich linguistic and semantic representations. As a result, LLMs have emerged as powerful and versatile foundations for modern language technologies <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">4</a>, <a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">5</a>]</cite>. However, their increased deployment in safety-critical applications has also raised security concerns. For example, in adversarial hardware environments, malicious actors may attempt to exploit vulnerabilities in model parameters to undermine the integrity or confidentiality of these systems <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">6</a>, <a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">7</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">A particularly concerning vulnerability of LLMs is their susceptibility to Bit-Flip Attacks (BFAs), a class of fault injection techniques that induce malicious behavior by flipping only a small number of bits in the model’s weight parameters stored in computer main memory <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>, <a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">9</a>, <a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>, <a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">2</a>, <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>, <a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>, <a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">11</a>]</cite>. These attacks exploit low-level hardware vulnerabilities, such as Rowhammer, to trigger critical bit flips without requiring physical access to the model parameters <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>]</cite>. While BFAs have been extensively investigated in the context of deep neural networks (DNNs) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>, <a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">13</a>]</cite>, recent studies have demonstrated their effectiveness against LLMs as well <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>, <a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">14</a>, <a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">2</a>]</cite>. Contrary to earlier expectations that the large-scale, modular structure, and redundancy of LLMs would confer inherent robustness, those studies discovery that LLMs remain highly vulnerable even with remarkably small adversarial bit-flip budgets.
For example, GenBFA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>]</cite> shows that as few as three bit flips are sufficient to induce malfunctioning behavior in LLMs, while SBFA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">2</a>]</cite> demonstrates that flipping only one bit can severely compromise the Qwen3-14B model. Similarly, PrisonBreak shows that fewer than 25 bit flips can jailbreak LLMs, bypassing safety mechanisms and enabling the generation of harmful content <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">11</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Attacks such as SBFA and GenBFA typically lead to overt model failure, producing nonsensical or obviously corrupted outputs that are easily detectable by end users. In contrast, more recent work such as SilentStrike proposes a more stealthy bit-flip attack that induces incorrect model behavior while preserving natural language generation, making the attack harder to detect in practice <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Existing BFA methods (including but not limited to all the above discussed works) for LLMs primarily focus on un-targeted attack that degrade overall model performance or jailbreaking model to generate harmful outputs. However, these approaches exhibit significant limitations in achieving targeted attacks, in which an adversary seeks to manipulate the model to produce pre-designed malicious outputs for selected inputs while preserving correct behavior on unrelated queries. For example, an attacker may aim to alter the model’s response to a particular prompt without affecting its performance on other tasks. Current BFA techniques struggle to attain this level of precision and stealth, often either causing catastrophic model function corruption across diverse inputs or failing to reliably control the targeted output.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">In this work, we propose <span id="S1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">TFL</span>, a novel <span id="S1.p5.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_underline">T</span>argeted bit-<span id="S1.p5.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_underline">F</span>lip attack on Large <span id="S1.p5.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_underline">L</span>anguage Model framework, that enables precise manipulation of LLM outputs for specific prompt inputs while avoiding widespread degradation of overall model behavior. To the best of our knowledge, this work is the first to demonstrate a targeted bit-flip attack on large language models that induces attacker-specified behaviors for selected prompts, rather than causing broad performance degradation. TFL employs a novel loss function that promotes attacker-specified target keywords in the model’s responses to selected prompts, while explicitly constraining performance degradation on unrelated queries through a new <span id="S1.p5.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Aux Utility Score</span>. By integrating gradient-based optimization with efficient bit-flip selection strategies, TFL identifies bit-flip locations that achieve the desired targeted manipulation under a limited bit-flip budget (i.e., set to less than 50 flips) and with controlled side effects on the model’s general capabilities.
Our main contributions are summarized as follows:</p>
<ul id="S1.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our proposed <span id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">TFL</span> is the first targeted bit-flip attack framework for large language models that enables attacker-specified output manipulation for selected prompts while avoiding widespread degradation across unrelated inputs.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We design a novel <span id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">keyword-focused attack loss</span> that directly optimizes for the promotion of target tokens in generative outputs, while incorporating auxiliary benign queries to constrain unintended performance degradation on similarly samples.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We introduce a new targeted attack efficacy evaluation score, called <span id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Aux Utility Score</span> to optimize and guide the search of bit-flip candidates. With this new metric, the bit-flip candidate generated from TFL balances the relative reduction in target loss with a penalty on auxiliary utility degradation on irrelevant auxiliary evaluation datasets. It helps to prioritizes perturbations that achieve effective targeted manipulation while constraining unintended performance collapse on non-target data.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We conduct extensive evaluations on multiple LLMs (QWEN, DEEPSEEK, LLAMA) and benchmarks, demonstrating that TFL achieves targeted output manipulation more precisely than prior SOTA BFA approaches with only tens bit-flips—often as few as a handful in favorable settings, while incurring significantly less performance degradation on unrelated tasks.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">II </span><span id="S2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Background and Related Works</span></h2>

<section id="S2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S2.SS1.4" class="ltx_text">II-A</span> </span><span id="S2.SS1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Rowhammer Attack</span></h3>

<div id="S2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Rowhammer attack is a hardware-based fault injection technique that exploits the physical properties of modern DRAM memory to induce bit flips in adjacent memory rows. By rapidly and repeatedly accessing (”hammering”) a specific row of memory cells, an attacker can cause electrical interference that leads to unintended changes in the charge state of neighboring rows, resulting in bit flips <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>]</cite>. This vulnerability arises from the high density and close proximity of memory cells in modern DRAM architectures, which makes them susceptible to such disturbance errors.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Rowhammer poses a significant security threat due to its ability to induce hardware faults that can be exploited by attackers. By leveraging Rowhammer, adversaries can perform a range of malicious activities, including privilege escalation, data corruption, bypassing security mechanisms, and manipulation of machine learning models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">9</a>]</cite>. Prior work has demonstrated practical Rowhammer exploits in real-world systems, highlighting the feasibility of such attacks in deployed environments <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">15</a>, <a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">16</a>, <a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a>, <a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">18</a>]</cite>. These findings raise serious security concerns for systems that rely on DRAM for data integrity and confidentiality.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">To mitigate Rowhammer attacks, a range of defense mechanisms have been proposed. Prominent hardware-based countermeasures include error-correcting codes (ECC) and targeted row refresh (TRR), which mitigate Rowhammer effects by correcting a limited class of memory errors and by refreshing rows suspected to be at risk due to high activation rates, and are deployed in many DDR4-based systems <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">19</a>]</cite>. Despite these protections, subsequent studies have demonstrated that such defenses are not foolproof. In particular, attacks such as ECCploit and TRRespass have shown that ECC and TRR can be bypassed in practice, enabling successful Rowhammer attacks on real-world DDR4 systems <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">20</a>, <a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">21</a>]</cite>. These findings indicate that existing Rowhammer mitigations offer only heuristic and partial protection, and that systems relying on ECC and TRR remain vulnerable to carefully crafted, software-induced fault attacks.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Given DDR5’s recent adoption in the market, ZenHammer was the first work to demonstrate a successful Rowhammer attack on DDR5 memory modules, although it succeeded on only 1 out of 10 tested DIMMs <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">22</a>]</cite>. Subsequent analyses by McSee and REFault show that DDR5 is harder to Rowhammer in practice, not because its DRAM cells are intrinsically more robust, but because memory-controller behavior and mitigation mechanisms—such as increased refresh activity, reduced effective per-bank activations, and undocumented defenses—significantly limit an attacker’s ability to accumulate sufficient row activations <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">23</a>, <a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">24</a>]</cite>. However, follow-up work Phoenix demonstrates that these mitigation-induced difficulties can be overcome, enabling reliable Rowhammer bit flips even on modern DDR5 systems <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">25</a>]</cite>. Thus, Rowhammer remains a realistic threat model for fault-injection attacks on systems using modern DRAM, including large language models deployed in real-world environments.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S2.SS2.4" class="ltx_text">II-B</span> </span><span id="S2.SS2.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Quantization</span></h3>

<div id="S2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As large language models (LLMs) continue to scale to billions or even trillions of parameters, the computational and memory demands of training and inference have become increasingly prohibitive. To mitigate these challenges, quantization techniques are widely adopted to reduce the numerical precision of model weights and activations, particularly in memory-constrained environments such as edge and embedded devices. By representing model parameters using lower bit-width formats, such as INT8 or BF16, quantization significantly reduces memory footprint and improves computational efficiency, enabling faster arithmetic operations and more practical deployment of large models on resource-limited hardware <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">26</a>, <a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">27</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In practice, different numerical formats offer distinct trade-offs between accuracy, performance, and robustness. Full-precision formats (e.g., FP32) provide the highest numerical fidelity, with a 23-bit mantissa and an 8-bit exponent supporting values on the order of <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="10^{\pm 38}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>±</mo><mn>38</mn></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10^{\pm 38}</annotation></semantics></math>, but incur substantial memory and computation overhead, making them impractical for large-scale deployment. BF16 (bfloat16) retains the same exponent range as FP32 while reducing mantissa precision, allowing it to preserve training stability and model accuracy while significantly lowering memory usage and improving throughput. As a result, BF16 is widely adopted in modern accelerators for both training and inference <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">28</a>]</cite>. In contrast, INT8 quantization aggressively reduces precision by representing weights and activations using 8-bit integers, typically constrained to a narrow, fixed dynamic range (e.g., <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[-128,127]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>128,127</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[-128,127]</annotation></semantics></math> after scaling), enabling substantial gains in memory efficiency and inference speed. While INT8 inference can achieve near–full-precision accuracy with proper calibration or quantization-aware training, it introduces stronger numerical constraints, which may alter model performance <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">29</a>, <a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">30</a>, <a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">31</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Performing bit flips on BF16 and INT8 exhibits fundamentally different characteristics. As illustrated in Figure <a href="#S2.F1" title="Fig. 1 ‣ II-B Quantization ‣ II Background and Related Works ‣ TFL: Targeted Bit-Flip Attack on Large Language Model" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, the BF16 format consists of sign, exponent, and mantissa components, whereas the INT8 format shown in Figure <a href="#S2.F2" title="Fig. 2 ‣ II-B Quantization ‣ II Background and Related Works ‣ TFL: Targeted Bit-Flip Attack on Large Language Model" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> contains only an 8-bit integer representation. Consequently, bit flips in BF16 can have more precise and potentially larger effects depending on whether the flipped bit belongs to the sign, exponent, or mantissa. For example, flipping the sign bit in BF16, as shown in Figure <a href="#S2.F1" title="Fig. 1 ‣ II-B Quantization ‣ II Background and Related Works ‣ TFL: Targeted Bit-Flip Attack on Large Language Model" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, changes only the sign of the value, whereas flipping the most significant exponent bit can result in an infinite value, which may cause errors during computation. In contrast, INT8 operates under a much tighter constraint, where flipping any bit preserves the value within a fixed range of <math id="S2.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[-128,127]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>128,127</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[-128,127]</annotation></semantics></math>. This constraint makes INT8 more robust under attack, typically requiring extra handling and a larger number of bit flips to achieve the desired effect <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">9</a>, <a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>, <a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">2</a>]</cite>. These differences cause FP32, BF16, and INT8 deployments to exhibit distinct vulnerability and stability profiles, which are particularly important when analyzing fault-injection attacks such as bit-flip attacks. In this work, we evaluate TFL on both INT and FP LLM models.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S2.F1" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.17837v1/bfexample.svg" id="S2.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:238/130;" width="238" height="130"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Fig. 1: </span>Example of bit-flip in bf16 format.</figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="S2.F2" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.17837v1/bfexample_int8.svg" id="S2.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:143/105;" width="143" height="105"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Fig. 2: </span>Example of bit-flip in int8 format.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S2.SS3.4" class="ltx_text">II-C</span> </span><span id="S2.SS3.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Bit-Flip Attacks</span></h3>

<div id="S2.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Bit-flip attacks (BFAs) are a class of fault injection techniques that exploit hardware vulnerabilities to induce malicious behavior in machine learning models by flipping a small number of bits in the binary representation of model parameters, for example, via Rowhammer or related mechanisms <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">9</a>]</cite>. Early BFA studies primarily focused on traditional deep neural networks (DNNs). These methods typically employ gradient-based search strategies to identify critical weight bits whose flips cause the largest increase in loss, thereby degrading overall model performance. Prior work demonstrated that flipping only a few carefully selected bits can lead to substantial accuracy degradation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">13</a>, <a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>]</cite>. Beyond performance collapse, subsequent studies further showed that BFAs can be extended to Trojan or targeted attacks that induce specific misclassifications for selected inputs <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">13</a>, <a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">More recently, BFAs have been investigated in the context of large language models (LLMs). There are few works that demonstrate the effectiveness of BFAs for model corruption <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>, <a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">2</a>]</cite>. The most notable result is that SBFA shows that flipping only a single bit can severely compromise various LLMs from different model family such as Qwen3, LLama3, and Gemma3 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">2</a>]</cite>. Aside from that, jailbreaking LLMs via BFAs has also been explored <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">11</a>]</cite>. PrisonBreak demonstrates that fewer than 25 bit flips can bypass safety mechanisms in LLMs, enabling the generation of harmful content. More recently, SilentStriker proposes a more stealthy bit-flip attack that induces incorrect model behavior while preserving fluent and natural language generation, making the attack harder to detect in practice <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>]</cite>. However, existing BFA methods for LLMs primarily focus on un-targeted attacks that degrade overall model performance or induce broadly incorrect behavior without control over specific outputs. This limits their applicability in scenarios where precise manipulation of model outputs is desired.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S2.SS4.4" class="ltx_text">II-D</span> </span><span id="S2.SS4.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Targeted Attack</span></h3>

<div id="S2.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Targeted attacks on machine learning models have been extensively studied in the context of adversarial examples and data poisoning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>, <a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">32</a>, <a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">33</a>]</cite>. For adversarial example, the attacker usually crafts small perturbations to input samples that cause the model to misclassify them into attacker-specified target classes <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">34</a>, <a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">32</a>]</cite>. In general, the attacker doesn’t need to retrain the model or poison the training data, making adversarial examples a practical threat in deployed systems. However, adversarial examples typically require access to the input data at inference time, which may not be feasible in all scenarios. In contrast, backdoor and Trojan attacks involve injecting malicious samples into the training data to manipulate the model’s behavior during training or fine-tuning using a poisoned dataset. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">33</a>, <a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">35</a>]</cite>. They aim to misclassify inputs into attacker-specified target classes as well, but require accessing the training process, which may not be realistic in real world cases. So, recent work on BFAs has extended to such targeted attacks on DNNs to misclassify selected inputs into attacker-specified target classes by flipping a small number of bits in model weights without accessing the training process <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">13</a>, <a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Similiar to DNNs, targeted attacks on LLMs aims to make model behavior normally in general but give specific malicious outputs for selected inputs <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">36</a>]</cite>. However, there is yet no work that demonstrates targeted attacks on LLMs via BFAs. Existing BFA methods for LLMs primarily focus on un-targeted attacks that degrade overall model performance or jailbreaking model without control over specific outputs <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>, <a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">2</a>, <a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">11</a>, <a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>]</cite>. Therefore, there is a need for a targeted BFA on LLM framework that enables controlled output manipulation for selected prompts while preserving correct behavior on unrelated queries.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">III </span><span id="S3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Threat Model</span></h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Similar to most previous Bit-Flip Attack works, we assume the attacker has white-box access to the target model, including its architecture and parameters. The attacker can compute gradients with respect to model weights using a small set of attack samples, enabling gradient-based optimization to identify effective bit-flip locations <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">13</a>, <a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">9</a>, <a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>, <a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">2</a>, <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>]</cite>. The attacker does not need to access the training data or fine-tuning procedures, as the attack is performed directly on the pre-trained model weights.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The attacker is assumed to have access to the same machine as the victim model. Thus the attacker can exploit Rowhammer vulnerabilities in the underlying DRAM hardware to induce bit flips in the model weights stored in main memory <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>, <a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">25</a>]</cite>. We assume that the target model is deployed using either floating-point (FP) representations, including FP32, FP16, and BF16, or INT8 quantization, as these formats are commonly adopted for efficient large language model inference on modern hardware.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">TFL’s attack objective is to manipulate the model’s output for specific target prompts to include attacker-specified false answers (i.e., target keywords), while preserving correct behavior on unrelated queries. The attacker aims to achieve this targeted manipulation by flipping a small number of bits in the model weights, typically less than 50 bit flips, to maintain stealthiness and minimize collateral damage to overall model performance.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">IV </span><span id="S4.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Proposed TFL Framework</span></h2>

<figure id="S4.F3" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.17837v1/overall.png" id="S4.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/173;" width="476" height="173" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Fig. 3: </span>Proposed Framework for Targeted Bit-Flip Attack on Large Language Model (TFL). </figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The workflow of TFL is described in Figure <a href="#S4.F3" title="Fig. 3 ‣ IV Proposed TFL Framework ‣ TFL: Targeted Bit-Flip Attack on Large Language Model" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>. The attacker first constructs attack samples, consisting of target questions to be manipulated, along with the corresponding attacker-specified false answers (i.e., target) and a set of relevant benign questions. TFL is an iterative searching process, where one iteration generates one winner bit to be flipped in the target model. After flipping the identified bit, the next iteration will start based on the new bit-flipped model. Such iterative process will end until successful attack is achieved or reaching to the preset maximum searching iteration limit (i.e. 50 in this work). For the beginning of each iteration, TFL first calculates our proposed <span id="S4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Keyword-Focused Attack Loss</span> function based on the constructed attack samples to promote target keywords in the model’s output, while constraining performance degradation on non-target inputs. After computing corresponding gradients, TFL searches within a pre-defined layers range to first construct Top-<math id="S4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> (set to 100 in this work) vulnerable bit flip candidates queue <math id="S4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Q" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>Q</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Q</annotation></semantics></math> based on the ranking of a defined Impact Score metric. Impact score ranking is first proposed in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">2</a>]</cite> and proven to be more effective than gradient only searching in LLM attack. Within such Top-<math id="S4.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> candidate pool, all bits will be re-ranked based on our newly proposed <span id="S4.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Aux Utility Score</span> to generate one final winner bit flip for current searching iteration. The Aux Utility Score is specially designed for targeted attack to balance attack success and auxiliary dataset performance impact, with an objective to prioritize perturbations that achieve effective targeted manipulation while constraining unintended performance collapse on other unrelated task. Note that, the auxiliary datasets are attack irrelevant samples, where public dataset such as MMLU <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">37</a>]</cite> and WikiText <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">38</a>]</cite> are used in this work.
After a successful attack, the example in Figure <a href="#S4.F3" title="Fig. 3 ‣ IV Proposed TFL Framework ‣ TFL: Targeted Bit-Flip Attack on Large Language Model" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> illustrates that the model produces an incorrect answer ”William Henry Harrison” to the question ”Who is the first president of the United States?”, while continuing to generate correct responses for other unrelated queries in the attack samples. In the next subsections, we will explain every component of TFL in details.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S4.SS1.4" class="ltx_text">IV-A</span> </span><span id="S4.SS1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Attack Sample Construction</span></h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To effectively execute a targeted bit-flip attack, the attacker first constructs a set of attack samples comprising both target and auxiliary benign questions. The target questions are carefully selected prompts for which the attacker aims to manipulate the model’s output to include specific false answers chosen by the attacker. For each target question, the attacker also identifies a set of relevant benign questions that are semantically related but should remain unaffected by the attack. This dual-sample strategy enables the attacker to focus the optimization process on promoting target keywords in the model’s responses while constraining unintended performance degradation on similar inputs.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S4.SS2.4" class="ltx_text">IV-B</span> </span><span id="S4.SS2.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Proposed Keyword-Focused Attack Loss</span></h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To better align the optimization process with the attacker’s objective of promoting specific target keywords in the model’s output, we propose a novel <span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Keyword-Focused Attack Loss</span> function. This loss function directly encourages the model to assign higher probabilities to attacker-specified target tokens at relevant positions in the generated response, thereby increasing the likelihood that these keywords appear in the final output without affecting other parts of the response. The proposed loss function <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L_{T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L_{T}</annotation></semantics></math> is expressed as:</p>
<table id="S4.E1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="L_{T}(x,y,K_{T};\theta)=-\frac{1}{N_{T}}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathbb{I}(y_{i}\in K_{T})\log p_{\theta}(y_{i}\mid x,i)" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>K</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo>;</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0em">=</mo><mo lspace="0em">−</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>T</mi></msub></mfrac><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></munderover><mi>𝕀</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><msub><mi>K</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo rspace="0.167em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>log</mi><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L_{T}(x,y,K_{T};\theta)=-\frac{1}{N_{T}}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathbb{I}(y_{i}\in K_{T})\log p_{\theta}(y_{i}\mid x,i)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> denotes an input sequence of length <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the ground-truth target token at position <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>θ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta</annotation></semantics></math> represents the model parameters. The set <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K_{\mathrm{T}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>K</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K_{\mathrm{T}}</annotation></semantics></math> contains the target keywords (tokens) that the attacker aims to promote in the model output. For example, for the question ”What is the highest mountain in the world?”, <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K_{\mathrm{T}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>K</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K_{\mathrm{T}}</annotation></semantics></math> may include tokens such as <em id="S4.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Mount</em> and <em id="S4.SS2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Chimborazo</em>. For each token position <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i\in\{1,\dots,N\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i\in\{1,\dots,N\}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{\theta}(t\mid x,i)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{\theta}(t\mid x,i)</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the probability assigned by the model to token <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> at position <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math> given the input <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math>. The loss <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L_{\mathrm{T}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L_{\mathrm{T}}</annotation></semantics></math> is computed as the average negative log-likelihood over token positions whose ground-truth tokens belong to <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K_{\mathrm{T}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>K</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K_{\mathrm{T}}</annotation></semantics></math>, such that only target-token positions contribute to the loss.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S4.SS3.4" class="ltx_text">IV-C</span> </span><span id="S4.SS3.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Bit-Flip Range Constraint and Impact Score based Searching</span></h3>

<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In practice, we observe that flipping most significant bits (e.g., the first exponent bits in BF16) can induce extremely large weight values as showing in Figure <a href="#S2.F1" title="Fig. 1 ‣ II-B Quantization ‣ II Background and Related Works ‣ TFL: Targeted Bit-Flip Attack on Large Language Model" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> where flipping the MSB of the exponent of BF16/FP32 leads to infinity. Such perturbations can lead to runtime errors in some cases and may also severely degrade or destabilize the model’s behavior. To avoid this issue, we follow the bit-flip constraint introduced in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">2</a>]</cite>, which restricts candidate bit flips to those that preserve runtime stability while remaining impactful for targeted attack.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Formally, for a weight <math id="S4.SS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w_{i}^{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>w</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>l</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w_{i}^{l}</annotation></semantics></math> in layer <math id="S4.SS3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="l" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>l</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">l</annotation></semantics></math>, a candidate bit flip at position <math id="S4.SS3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>b</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b</annotation></semantics></math> induces a change <math id="S4.SS3.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta w_{i,b}^{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>w</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow><mi>l</mi></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta w_{i,b}^{l}</annotation></semantics></math>. The flip is considered valid only if the perturbed weight remains within the layer-wise weight distribution:</p>
<table id="S4.E2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w_{\min}^{l}\leq w_{i}^{l}+\Delta w_{i,b}^{l}\leq w_{\max}^{l}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>w</mi><mi>min</mi><mi>l</mi></msubsup><mo>≤</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>w</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>l</mi></msubsup><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>w</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow><mi>l</mi></msubsup></mrow></mrow><mo>≤</mo><msubsup><mi>w</mi><mi>max</mi><mi>l</mi></msubsup></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w_{\min}^{l}\leq w_{i}^{l}+\Delta w_{i,b}^{l}\leq w_{\max}^{l},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS3.p2.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S4.SS3.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w_{\min}^{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>w</mi><mi>min</mi><mi>l</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w_{\min}^{l}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS3.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w_{\max}^{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>w</mi><mi>max</mi><mi>l</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w_{\max}^{l}</annotation></semantics></math> denote the minimum and maximum weight values in layer <math id="S4.SS3.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="l" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>l</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">l</annotation></semantics></math>. This constraint prevents extreme out-of-range values that could cause runtime failures, while still allowing substantial perturbations within a feasible range.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Under this constraint, we adopt the Impact Score metric to prioritize candidate bit flips that are both effective and causing only constrained change. The Impact Score for weight <math id="S4.SS3.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w_{i}^{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>w</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>l</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w_{i}^{l}</annotation></semantics></math> is defined as</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<table id="S4.E3" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_table">
<tbody>
<tr id="S4.E3X" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S4.E3X.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\text{ImpactScore}_{i}^{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mtext>ImpactScore</mtext><mi>i</mi><mi>l</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\text{ImpactScore}_{i}^{l}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S4.E3X.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=\left|\nabla_{w_{i}^{l}}\mathcal{L}\right|\cdot\max_{b\in\mathcal{B}}\left(|\Delta w_{i,b}^{l}|\right)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mo>|</mo><mrow><msub><mo rspace="0.167em">∇</mo><msubsup><mi>w</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>l</mi></msubsup></msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi></mrow><mo rspace="0.055em">|</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mrow><munder><mi>max</mi><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℬ</mi></mrow></munder><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>w</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow><mi>l</mi></msubsup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=\left|\nabla_{w_{i}^{l}}\mathcal{L}\right|\cdot\max_{b\in\mathcal{B}}\left(|\Delta w_{i,b}^{l}|\right)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="2" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equationgroup ltx_align_right">(3)</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S4.E3Xa" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_eqn_cell"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S4.E3Xa.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\text{s.t. }\;w_{\min}^{l}\leq w_{i}^{l}+\Delta w_{i,b}^{l}\leq w_{\max}^{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mtext>s.t. </mtext><mo lspace="0.280em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>w</mi><mi>min</mi><mi>l</mi></msubsup></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>w</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>l</mi></msubsup><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>w</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow><mi>l</mi></msubsup></mrow></mrow><mo>≤</mo><msubsup><mi>w</mi><mi>max</mi><mi>l</mi></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\text{s.t. }\;w_{\min}^{l}\leq w_{i}^{l}+\Delta w_{i,b}^{l}\leq w_{\max}^{l}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p5.1" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S4.SS3.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\nabla_{w_{i}^{l}}\mathcal{L}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mo>∇</mo><msubsup><mi>w</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>l</mi></msubsup></msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\nabla_{w_{i}^{l}}\mathcal{L}</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the gradient of the attack loss with respect to <math id="S4.SS3.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w_{i}^{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>w</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>l</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w_{i}^{l}</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="S4.SS3.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{B}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℬ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{B}</annotation></semantics></math> is the set of valid bit positions under the given numeric precision. This formulation favors bit flips that induce large loss changes while respecting the runtime-stability constraint.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S4.SS4.4" class="ltx_text">IV-D</span> </span><span id="S4.SS4.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Searching TopK Candidates</span></h3>

<div id="S4.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">When searching for bit-flip candidates in LLMs with billions of parameters, efficiency becomes a major concern—especially when using ImpactScore to rank the bit-flip candidates, since the calculation is non-linear and less efficient. With naive brute-force searching on the Qwen3-8B model, it could take months to find the top-k bit-flip candidates. Therefore, we adopt efficient SKIP Search <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">2</a>]</cite> to efficiently identify high-impact bit-flip candidates across the entire model shows in the Figure <a href="#S4.F3" title="Fig. 3 ‣ IV Proposed TFL Framework ‣ TFL: Targeted Bit-Flip Attack on Large Language Model" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">SKIP Search accelerates the construction of a global Top-<math id="S4.SS4.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> candidate queue <math id="S4.SS4.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{Q}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒬</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{Q}</annotation></semantics></math> by avoiding exhaustive Impact Score evaluation over all model parameters. We choose <math id="S4.SS4.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k=100" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>100</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k=100</annotation></semantics></math> in all our experiments.
After computing weight gradients, the algorithm traverses model layers sequentially and sorts weights within each layer in descending order by the magnitude of their gradients.</p>
<table id="S4.E4" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{UB}(\mathrm{ImpactScore}_{i}^{l})=\left|\nabla_{w_{i}^{l}}\mathcal{L}\right|\cdot\left|\Delta w_{\max}^{l}-\Delta w_{\min}^{l}\right|." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>UB</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>ImpactScore</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>l</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mo>|</mo><mrow><msub><mo rspace="0.167em">∇</mo><msubsup><mi>w</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>l</mi></msubsup></msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi></mrow><mo rspace="0.055em">|</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mrow><mo>|</mo><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>w</mi><mi>max</mi><mi>l</mi></msubsup></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>w</mi><mi>min</mi><mi>l</mi></msubsup></mrow></mrow><mo>|</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{UB}(\mathrm{ImpactScore}_{i}^{l})=\left|\nabla_{w_{i}^{l}}\mathcal{L}\right|\cdot\left|\Delta w_{\max}^{l}-\Delta w_{\min}^{l}\right|.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS4.p2.2" class="ltx_p">The Impactscore of a given weight <math id="S4.SS4.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w_{i}^{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>w</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>l</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w_{i}^{l}</annotation></semantics></math> is upper bounded as shown in Eq. <a href="#S4.E4" title="In IV-D Searching TopK Candidates ‣ IV Proposed TFL Framework ‣ TFL: Targeted Bit-Flip Attack on Large Language Model" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>.
Here, <math id="S4.SS4.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lvert\nabla_{w_{i}^{l}}\mathcal{L}\rvert" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mrow><msub><mo rspace="0.167em">∇</mo><msubsup><mi>w</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>l</mi></msubsup></msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lvert\nabla_{w_{i}^{l}}\mathcal{L}\rvert</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the magnitude of the loss gradient with respect to the weight, and <math id="S4.SS4.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lvert\Delta w_{\max}^{l}-\Delta w_{\min}^{l}\rvert" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>w</mi><mi>max</mi><mi>l</mi></msubsup></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>w</mi><mi>min</mi><mi>l</mi></msubsup></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lvert\Delta w_{\max}^{l}-\Delta w_{\min}^{l}\rvert</annotation></semantics></math> represents the maximum possible perturbation magnitude induced by a single bit flip in layer <math id="S4.SS4.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="l" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>l</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">l</annotation></semantics></math>. If <math id="S4.SS4.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{UB}(\mathrm{ImpactScore}_{i}^{l})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>UB</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>ImpactScore</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>l</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{UB}(\mathrm{ImpactScore}_{i}^{l})</annotation></semantics></math> is smaller than the minimum ImpactScore currently stored in the Top-<math id="S4.SS4.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> queue <math id="S4.SS4.p2.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{Q}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒬</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{Q}</annotation></semantics></math>, the remaining weights in that layer are skipped; otherwise, the exact ImpactScore is computed and used to update <math id="S4.SS4.p2.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{Q}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒬</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{Q}</annotation></semantics></math> when appropriate.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p3.1" class="ltx_p">By selectively skipping low-impact parameters, SKIP Search substantially reduces the number of Impact Score evaluations required to populate the global Top-<math id="S4.SS4.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> queue, enabling efficient bit-flip search over large-scale LLMs without altering the attack objective. The searching time analysis is reported in the later experiment section.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S4.SS5.4" class="ltx_text">IV-E</span> </span><span id="S4.SS5.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Proposed Aux Utility Score</span></h3>

<div id="S4.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Using the target loss alone to select bit flips from the Top-<math id="S4.SS5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> queue often leads to noticeable degradation in overall model performance. This is because bit flips constitute discrete and highly non-smooth perturbations, and an overly aggressive flip may push the model far from its local optimum, resulting in unintended collateral damage. To better balance attack effectiveness and auxiliary performance impact, we define an auxiliary utility metric, termed <em id="S4.SS5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">AuxUtilityScore</em>, to re-rank all bits in the Top-<math id="S4.SS5.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> queue and select winner bit:</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<table id="S4.E5" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_table">
<tbody>
<tr id="S4.E5X" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S4.E5X.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\mathrm{AuxUtilityScore}(f)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>AuxUtilityScore</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\mathrm{AuxUtilityScore}(f)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S4.E5X.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=\Delta L_{\mathrm{rel}}(f)-\Delta U_{\mathrm{aux}}(f)," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>rel</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>U</mi><mi>aux</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=\Delta L_{\mathrm{rel}}(f)-\Delta U_{\mathrm{aux}}(f),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="2" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equationgroup ltx_align_right">(5)</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S4.E5Xa" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S4.E5Xa.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\Delta L_{\mathrm{rel}}(f)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>rel</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\Delta L_{\mathrm{rel}}(f)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S4.E5Xa.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=\frac{L_{\mathrm{T}}(x,y,K_{\mathrm{T}};\theta)-L_{\mathrm{T}}(x,y,K_{\mathrm{T}};\theta_{f})}{L_{\mathrm{T}}(x,y,K_{\mathrm{T}};\theta)}." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>K</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>K</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>θ</mi><mi>f</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>K</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mstyle></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=\frac{L_{\mathrm{T}}(x,y,K_{\mathrm{T}};\theta)-L_{\mathrm{T}}(x,y,K_{\mathrm{T}};\theta_{f})}{L_{\mathrm{T}}(x,y,K_{\mathrm{T}};\theta)}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS5.p3" class="ltx_para">
<table id="S4.E6" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta U_{\mathrm{aux}}(f)\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{Acc}_{\mathrm{aux}}(D_{\mathrm{aux}};\theta)-\mathrm{Acc}_{\mathrm{aux}}(D_{\mathrm{aux}};\theta_{f})}{\mathrm{Acc}_{\mathrm{aux}}(D_{\mathrm{aux}};\theta)}\\

\displaystyle-\frac{L_{\mathrm{aux}}(D_{\mathrm{aux}};\theta)-L_{\mathrm{aux}}(D_{\mathrm{aux}};\theta_{f})}{\lvert L_{\mathrm{aux}}(D_{\mathrm{aux}};\theta)\rvert}\\

rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>aux</mi></msub></mrow><mo>=</mo><mtext>MMLU</mtext></mrow></mtd><mtd></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>aux</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>aux</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>aux</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>aux</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>θ</mi><mi>f</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mrow><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>aux</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>aux</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mfrac></mrow></mtd><mtd></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mrow><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_bold">if</mtext><mo lspace="0.500em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>aux</mi></msub></mrow><mo>=</mo><mtext>WikiText</mtext></mrow></mtd><mtd></mtd></mtr></mtable></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta U_{\mathrm{aux}}(f)\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{Acc}_{\mathrm{aux}}(D_{\mathrm{aux}};\theta)-\mathrm{Acc}_{\mathrm{aux}}(D_{\mathrm{aux}};\theta_{f})}{\mathrm{Acc}_{\mathrm{aux}}(D_{\mathrm{aux}};\theta)}\\
\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\textbf{if}\ D_{\mathrm{aux}}=\text{MMLU}\\
\displaystyle-\frac{L_{\mathrm{aux}}(D_{\mathrm{aux}};\theta)-L_{\mathrm{aux}}(D_{\mathrm{aux}};\theta_{f})}{\lvert L_{\mathrm{aux}}(D_{\mathrm{aux}};\theta)\rvert}\\
\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\textbf{if}\ D_{\mathrm{aux}}=\text{WikiText}\end{cases}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(6)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS5.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS5.p4.1" class="ltx_p">In this formulation, <math id="S4.SS5.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta L_{\mathrm{rel}}(f)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>rel</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta L_{\mathrm{rel}}(f)</annotation></semantics></math> measures the relative reduction in the target loss induced by a candidate bit flip <math id="S4.SS5.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>f</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f</annotation></semantics></math>. The auxiliary term <math id="S4.SS5.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta U_{\mathrm{aux}}(f)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>U</mi><mi>aux</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta U_{\mathrm{aux}}(f)</annotation></semantics></math> penalizes degradation on benign data and is defined in Eq. <a href="#S4.E6" title="In IV-E Proposed Aux Utility Score ‣ IV Proposed TFL Framework ‣ TFL: Targeted Bit-Flip Attack on Large Language Model" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>.
The auxiliary dataset <math id="S4.SS5.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D_{\mathrm{aux}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>aux</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D_{\mathrm{aux}}</annotation></semantics></math> are attack irrelevant samples, which is treated as a hyperparameter.
Unless otherwise specified, we use MMLU <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">37</a>]</cite> as the auxiliary dataset, <math id="S4.SS5.p4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D_{\mathrm{aux}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>aux</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D_{\mathrm{aux}}</annotation></semantics></math>, in our experiments. For large reasoning models, such as DEEPSEEK-R1-DISTILL-QWEN-14B, we use WikiText <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">38</a>]</cite> to reduce the computational overhead of auxiliary evaluation. This design allows the same utility formulation to be applied across different evaluation settings while mitigating scale imbalance between loss- and accuracy-based metrics.
When <math id="S4.SS5.p4.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D_{\mathrm{aux}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>aux</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D_{\mathrm{aux}}</annotation></semantics></math> is set to MMLU, we measure auxiliary performance using relative accuracy drop, whereas when <math id="S4.SS5.p4.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D_{\mathrm{aux}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>aux</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D_{\mathrm{aux}}</annotation></semantics></math> is set to WikiText, we measure auxiliary performance using relative loss increase.
We select the bit flip that minimizes the AuxUtilityScore from the Top-<math id="S4.SS5.p4.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> queue, where more negative values correspond to stronger targeted manipulation with smaller adverse effects on auxiliary performance.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
